Human factors and ergonomics:
# Human factors and ergonomics
## Ergonomics
Ergonomics is the study of how people interact with products and environments. Designers use anthropometric data, which are measurements of the human body, to size products for the intended users.

## Percentiles
Designers often design for the 5th to 95th percentile of users, which covers 90 percent of a population. A door height is designed for the tallest users and a reach distance for the shortest.

## Psychological and physiological factors
Physiological factors include comfort, strength and fatigue. Psychological factors include how users perceive colour, light, sound and the meaning of controls.

## Key terms
Ergonomics: the study of how people interact with products and environments
Anthropometrics: measurements of the human body used in design
Percentile: the value below which a given percentage of a population falls
User-centred design: design that puts the needs of users at the centre of each stage
Physiological factors: factors relating to how the body works, such as comfort and fatigue
Resource management and sustainable prod:
# Resource management and sustainable production
## Resources
Renewable resources can be replaced naturally; non-renewable resources such as oil and metals cannot. Designers reduce waste by choosing materials carefully and designing for disassembly.

## The circular economy
In a circular economy products are designed to be reused, repaired, remanufactured or recycled, rather than made, used and thrown away in a linear economy.

## Life cycle analysis
Life cycle analysis measures the environmental impact of a product from raw materials through production, distribution, use and disposal.

## Key terms
Circular economy: an economic model that keeps materials in use through reuse and recycling
Life cycle analysis: an assessment of a product’s environmental impact from cradle to grave
Design for disassembly: designing a product so it can be taken apart for repair or recycling
Renewable resource: a resource that can be naturally replaced
Eco-design: design that reduces environmental impact
Modelling and prototyping:
# Modelling and prototyping
## Types of model
Designers use sketches, 2D drawings, physical models, mock-ups and computer-aided design (CAD) models to develop and test ideas. A prototype is an early working version used for testing.

## Why model
Models communicate ideas to clients and test function, form and ergonomics before expensive production. Rapid prototyping such as 3D printing makes physical models directly from CAD files.

## Key terms
Prototype: an early working version of a product used for testing
CAD: computer-aided design software used to create digital models
Mock-up: a full-size model used to test appearance and ergonomics
Rapid prototyping: making physical models quickly from digital files, such as 3D printing
Orthographic drawing: a drawing showing an object from front, side and top views
Materials and their properties:
# Materials and their properties
## Material groups
Materials include metals, timbers, polymers, ceramics, composites and textiles. Thermoplastics can be reshaped when heated; thermosetting plastics cannot.

## Properties
Physical properties include density and conductivity. Mechanical properties include tensile strength, hardness, toughness, stiffness and ductility. Designers choose materials by matching properties to the product’s needs and cost.

## Composites and smart materials
Composites such as carbon fibre combine materials for better properties. Smart materials change in response to their environment, such as shape memory alloys and thermochromic pigments.

## Key terms
Tensile strength: the ability of a material to resist being pulled apart
Thermoplastic: a polymer that can be reheated and reshaped
Composite: a material made by combining two or more materials
Smart material: a material whose properties change in response to its surroundings
Ductility: the ability to be drawn out without breaking
Innovation and markets:
# Innovation and markets
## Invention and innovation
An invention is a new idea or device. An innovation is an invention that is successfully brought to market. Innovation can be incremental, improving an existing product, or radical, creating something new.

## Product life cycle
Products go through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Companies use redesign and marketing to extend the maturity stage.

## Diffusion
The diffusion of innovations describes how products spread from innovators and early adopters to the majority and laggards.

## Key terms
Innovation: an invention that has been successfully brought to market
Incremental innovation: a small improvement to an existing product
Radical innovation: a breakthrough that creates a new product or market
Product life cycle: the stages of introduction, growth, maturity and decline
Early adopter: a consumer who buys a new product soon after launch
Commercial production:
# Commercial production
## Scales of production
One-off production makes a single item to order. Batch production makes a set number of identical items. Mass production makes large numbers on an assembly line. Continuous flow runs non-stop.

## Manufacturing systems
Just-in-time production keeps little stock and orders parts when needed. Computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) uses computers to control machines for accuracy and repeatability. Quality control checks products against standards.

## Key terms
Batch production: making a set quantity of identical products
Mass production: making large numbers of products on an assembly line
Just-in-time: a system that receives parts only as they are needed
CAM: computer-aided manufacturing
Quality control: checking products meet a set standard
Design project:
# Design project
## What it is
The internal assessment is a design project in which the student identifies a problem, researches users, writes a design brief and specification, develops and tests solutions, and evaluates the final product.

## Doing it well
Write measurable specification points, generate a range of ideas, record user testing, and evaluate the solution against the specification with suggestions for improvement.

## Key terms
Design brief: a short statement of the problem and the intended outcome
Design specification: a list of measurable requirements the solution must meet
Iteration: repeating cycles of design, testing and improvement
User testing: testing a design with intended users to gather feedback
Evaluation: judging how well a solution meets its specification
